Squatters and the law in Nevada

A squatter has no automatic right to a Nevada house. Title can pass by adverse possession only after a long, open and continuous claim that meets several statutes at once, and an unauthorized occupant can be removed through a court process the law spells out.

The word squatter covers very different situations: someone who walked into a vacant house, a former tenant who stayed after a lease ended, an heir living in a parent's home, or a person let in by a fake landlord. Nevada treats each one differently. A tenant who stays after notice falls under the landlord-tenant chapters. A person who never had permission is handled as an unlawful or unauthorized occupant.

Before you do anything else, work out which of these you are dealing with. That choice decides the notice you serve and the court you file in.

What adverse possession requires

A claimant has to meet requirements in more than one section of NRS chapter 11, and the tax requirement is the one many people overlook.

  • Five years of occupation. NRS 11.150 requires, in addition to the requirements of NRS 11.120 or 11.140, that the land was occupied and claimed for 5 years, continuously.
  • Payment of taxes. The same section requires that the claimant or predecessors paid all state, county and municipal taxes levied and assessed for that period, or tendered payment.
  • Possession in a recognized form. For a claim not founded on a written instrument, NRS 11.140 treats land as possessed only when it has been protected by a substantial enclosure or has been usually cultivated or improved.

NRS 11.070 backs up the five year frame from the owner's side. No cause of action founded on title to real property is effective unless the party or a predecessor was seized or possessed of the premises within 5 years before the act in question. An owner who pays the tax and watches the property makes the claimant's job much harder, since the claimant must show the taxes were paid or tendered.

Someone who moved into a vacant house last month will not meet these tests. A claim can still cloud title, though, and a clouded title is hard to sell. If a claim has been made against your house, tell a title company early.

Removing an unauthorized occupant

Use the court. Nevada has a civil removal process that an owner can use whether or not anyone has been arrested. It is built around a 4 day notice to surrender, and the Civil Law Self-Help Center in Clark County can walk you through the forms.

StepWhat happens
1. Notice to SurrenderA 4 judicial day notice, which does not count the day of service, Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays or holidays
2. ServicePersonally in front of a witness; or with a person of suitable age and discretion plus mailing; or posting plus mailing, in that order
3. Occupant respondsLeaves, or files an affidavit with a legal defense by the end of the fourth judicial day
4. Owner's complaintFiled with the Justice Court with the notice and proof of service attached; the filing fee is $71
5. Court reviewA hearing within 7 judicial days if a defense is raised; otherwise a removal order, carried out by the constable or sheriff within 24 hours

The notice must name the court, tell the occupant about the right to oppose it by affidavit, warn that a summary order could lead to removal within 24 hours, and say that the owner will provide safe storage of belongings for 21 days at the occupant's cost. An occupant can ask the court for up to 20 more days to move, but only in the answer filed within the four day window.

Keep your proof of service with the complaint. A notice served out of order or without the required wording gives the occupant an easy argument, and you can lose days restarting.

When can an owner change the locks after an arrest?

NRS 40.412 gives an owner a faster route in one narrow case: all known unlawful or unauthorized adult occupants have been arrested for housebreaking or unlawful occupancy, and any minor occupants have been taken into State custody. Only then may the owner retake possession and change the locks.

Strict conditions come with it. When the locks are changed, the owner or an authorized representative must post a written notice on the dwelling that identifies the address, the court with jurisdiction, and the date possession was retaken. The notice stays posted at least 21 calendar days, and a copy goes to the court within 1 day after the locks change, with an address for service.

  • The occupant has 21 calendar days to contest by filing a verified complaint for reentry.
  • Reentry without a court order is a criminal offense, punishable by up to 4 years in prison.
  • The owner must provide safe storage of remaining personal property and can dispose of it after 21 calendar days unless the occupant files an affidavit under NRS 40.414.
  • The section does not apply if any unlawful or unauthorized occupant is still in the dwelling.

Owners miss that last point most often. If someone is still living there, you cannot change the locks under this section.

A tenant who stays versus a squatter

A tenant is someone who entered with permission under a lease or agreement, and the notice rules differ. Under NRS 40.2516, a tenant who fails to perform a condition of the lease and does not comply within 5 days after written notice is guilty of an unlawful detainer, and the landlord may then seek possession under the summary eviction statutes.

That is a different clock and a different notice from the 4 judicial day surrender notice for an unauthorized occupant. Use the notice that matches the occupant's status. Our Nevada landlord tenant guide covers the tenant side.

If the occupant is a relative who moved into an inherited house, or someone who says they were promised the property, talk to an attorney. Those claims sometimes rest on documents or payments, and the quick removal process is built for people with no right at all.

Selling a house with an occupant in it

An occupied house can still sell, but the buyer needs a clear path to possession. A traditional buyer with a lender usually wants an appraisal, an inspection and a vacant property at closing, and an unauthorized occupant can stall every one of those steps.

Start with three facts: who is living there, what paper they hold, and who the county shows as owner of record. The recorder's records and the treasurer's account will tell you whether the tax is current. That matters because the five year tax requirement in NRS 11.150 works in your favor when you have paid.

  1. Document the occupancy with photos, dates and any police report numbers.
  2. Keep the property taxes current, and keep the receipts.
  3. Choose the right notice, civil removal or tenant eviction, and serve it exactly as the court rules require.
  4. Do not turn off utilities, remove belongings or change locks outside NRS 40.412 without legal advice.

Expect to hand a buyer or title company the tax receipts, the notice, proof of service and any court papers. Those documents show the occupant is on the way out or already gone, and a buyer will ask for them.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in Nevada?

The statute requires 5 years of continuous occupation and claim, plus payment of all taxes levied for that period, or a tender of payment (NRS 11.150). Possession must also meet NRS 11.140 if no written instrument is involved.

Can a squatter claim my Nevada house if I pay the property taxes?

The claimant must show that taxes for the 5 year period were paid by the claimant or predecessors, or tendered. If the owner paid them, that requirement is hard to meet (NRS 11.150).

Can I change the locks on an occupied Nevada house?

Not under NRS 40.412 while any unlawful or unauthorized occupant is still living there. The section applies only after all known adult occupants have been arrested and minors taken into State custody, and reentry without a court order can be a crime.

How fast can an unauthorized occupant be removed in Nevada?

After the 4 judicial day notice and a Justice Court complaint, the constable serves a removal order requiring the occupant to leave within 24 hours. A hearing may be set within 7 judicial days if the occupant raises a defense.

Who stores belongings left in the home after a Nevada removal?

The owner must provide safe storage for 21 days, and the occupant pays reasonable inventory, moving and storage costs before getting the property back (NRS 40.412).

Which Nevada laws cover a rented house

Two parts of the Nevada Revised Statutes matter. Chapter 118A is the landlord and tenant law for dwellings. Chapter 40 sets the court procedures for removing a tenant.

Chapter 118A covers the rental agreement, deposits, rent increases, repairs and what each side owes. Chapter 40 covers notices to surrender and the summary eviction process after a tenant defaults or a tenancy ends.

A rental agreement cannot waive a tenant's rights under the chapter. NRS 118A.220 lists prohibited provisions, including a tenant agreeing to give up rights or remedies, authorizing someone to confess judgment, or agreeing to pay the landlord's attorney's fees, other than a clause awarding reasonable fees to the prevailing party.

What happens to the lease when the owner sells?

The lease continues. Under NRS 118A.349, when the property is sold voluntarily, the new owner steps into the previous owner's rights and obligations under the rental agreement, and the tenant keeps the tenant's own, unless the new owner and the tenant agree to change or end the lease.

The new owner must send the tenant a notice within 30 days after the sale. It gives the new owner's contact information for rent, says the existing agreement continues through the tenancy, states the amount held as a security deposit, and warns that failing to pay rent to the new owner or to follow the lease is a breach.

A seller with a tenant should plan for these points:

  • The buyer inherits a lease that may have months left, so rent, term and any renewal clauses belong in the sale paperwork.
  • The deposit must follow the property, covered in the next section.
  • If the buyer wants the house empty, a deal with the tenant is the clean path. The statute leaves room for the new owner and tenant to modify or end the lease by agreement.

The security deposit at sale

Before recording the deed, the landlord must either hand the remaining deposit to the buyer in writing or tell the buyer in writing that the deposit went back to the tenant. NRS 118A.244 sets that rule. It also requires the successor to accept the deposit, and bars the successor from demanding an additional one during the term of the rental agreement.

When the landlord's interest ends by sale, the landlord must within a reasonable time do one of two things. One is to notify the tenant in writing of the successor's name, address and telephone number and that the deposit balance was transferred. The other is to return the remaining deposit to the tenant. Either step ends the landlord's further liability for the deposit.

An owner who skips this takes on real exposure. A landlord who fails to return the remainder within 30 days after a tenancy ends owes damages equal to the entire deposit, plus a further sum the court fixes of up to the amount of the deposit under NRS 118A.242.

Limits a Nevada landlord should know

These limits come straight from chapter 118A, and a buyer's lawyer will check each one during a sale.

TopicRule
Security deposit cap3 months' periodic rent, including last month's rent (NRS 118A.242)
Return of depositItemized accounting and remainder within 30 days after the tenancy ends (NRS 118A.242)
Rent increase notice60 days written notice, or 30 days for periodic tenancies under 1 month (NRS 118A.300)
Late feeNot before 3 calendar days after the due date, and no more than 5 percent of periodic rent (NRS 118A.210)
Landlord entryAt least 24 hours notice, at reasonable times, except in an emergency (NRS 118A.330)
Cure period for a landlord's habitability or lease breach14 days after written notice (NRS 118A.350, 118A.355)
Unlawful lockout or utility shutoffActual damages or up to $2,500 fixed by the court, or both (NRS 118A.390)

Showing the house to buyers while a tenant lives there

You can, with notice. Under NRS 118A.330 a tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for the landlord to enter to show the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, among other purposes. The landlord must give at least 24 hours' notice and may enter only at reasonable times during normal business hours, unless the tenant agrees to shorter notice or to entry outside business hours.

Emergencies are the exception, and a landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

Put the showing schedule in writing and keep it modest, because the 24 hour rule applies to each entry.

Ending a tenancy before you sell

Only through the notice and court steps the statutes set out, and the right notice depends on the tenancy type and the reason. Under NRS 40.251, a tenant in a dwelling under chapter 118A is guilty of unlawful detainer after the lease term ends or is terminated and a notice period expires. That period is at least 7 days for week-to-week tenancies and at least 30 days for other periodic tenancies. A 5 day notice applies where the tenant failed to perform basic or contractual obligations under chapter 118A.

For unpaid rent, NRS 40.253 provides a written notice requiring payment or surrender by the close of business on the seventh judicial day after service. Under NRS 40.2516, a tenant who fails to perform another lease condition after written notice has 5 days to comply or leave.

Serve notices by the methods in NRS 40.280, which include delivery by the sheriff, a constable, a process server or an attorney's agent. A fixed-term lease does not end just because the owner lists the house, and NRS 118A.349 confirms the lease follows the property.

What a landlord may not do

Self-help is off the table. NRS 118A.480 allows possession to be recovered only through an action for possession or similar proceeding, when the tenant surrenders, or when the tenant abandons the unit. Under NRS 118A.390, unlawfully removing a tenant, blocking entry or willfully cutting essential services lets the tenant recover possession, actual damages, or an amount of up to $2,500 fixed by the court.

A tenant may file a verified complaint for expedited relief within 5 judicial days after the unlawful act.

NRS 118A.460 governs property left behind. The landlord must provide safe storage for 30 days after abandonment or eviction, and may charge reasonable costs of inventory, moving and storage. After that, the landlord may dispose of the property if reasonable efforts were made to find the tenant, written notice of intent to dispose was given, and at least 14 days have gone by since the notice. NRS 118A.520 abolishes distraint for rent.

Repairs and habitability

A dwelling must be habitable at all times. NRS 118A.290 defines habitability by housing and health codes and by basics such as a weatherproof roof and walls and working plumbing, water, heating and electrical systems. A landlord also may not charge fees for repairs or maintenance that are the landlord's own duty.

The tenant's remedies come in stages. After written notice, the landlord has 14 days to fix a remediable failure or make best efforts. If the landlord does not, the tenant may end the lease, recover actual damages, ask the court for relief, or under NRS 118A.355 withhold rent without late fees until the problem is remedied or a good faith attempt is made. For a small repair costing less than $100 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, NRS 118A.360 lets a tenant who has notified the landlord make the repair and deduct the reasonable cost from rent, up to that amount.

A tenant cannot use these remedies for conditions the tenant or a guest caused. Keep written records of repair requests and fixes, since a buyer will ask for them.

If the seller stays after closing

A person who sold the property and keeps living there can be removed after a 3-day written notice to surrender, once title under the sale has been perfected. NRS 40.255 includes a sale by the person, or by someone the person claims under, among the cases where a holdover can be removed through the court procedures in NRS 40.290 to 40.420.

That matters for a seller who wants a short rent-back after a cash sale. Put the rent-back in a written agreement with a clear end date, rent amount and deposit, because the occupant becomes a holdover if the arrangement ends and the person stays.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Nevada tenant have to move when the owner sells the house?

No. Under NRS 118A.349 the lease continues with the new owner unless the new owner and the tenant agree to change or end it. The new owner must send the tenant a notice within 30 days after the sale.

How much can a Nevada landlord charge for a security deposit?

A security deposit and surety bond together, including last month's rent, cannot exceed 3 months' periodic rent under NRS 118A.242. The remainder, with an itemized accounting, is due within 30 days after the tenancy ends.

How much notice must a Nevada landlord give before raising rent?

Written notice 60 days before the first rental payment to be increased, or 30 days for a periodic tenancy of less than one month, under NRS 118A.300.

How long does an eviction notice take for unpaid rent in Nevada?

NRS 40.253 provides a written notice to pay or surrender by the close of business on the seventh judicial day after service. A shorter period applies to certain weekly tenancies of no more than 45 days. The case then goes through the court.

Can a landlord change the locks or shut off utilities to clear a house for sale?

No. NRS 118A.480 requires a court process or a surrender or abandonment. Under NRS 118A.390 a locked-out tenant, or one whose essential services are cut, can recover possession, actual damages, or up to $2,500 as fixed by the court.
